In data in (3.8) we notice that in the case of trisyllables if the penult is heavy and antepenult is light, the penult is stressed; otherwise the antepenult receives main stress. Facts like these provide a clinching piece of evidence in support of contending that SHB is partially quantity sensitive. [p. 146] ... The metrical rules of disyllabic words indicate that first syllable always attracts stress.In trisyllabic words, if the penult is heavy and antepenult is light then penult attracts stress otherwise antepenultimate receives stress which implies SHB is partially quantity sensitive. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (54 pp., Nitro Pro text layer, no scanned needed; PDF pages 1-54 = thesis pp. 116-169, chapter heading 'CHAPTER 3 FOOT IN SYLHETI BANGLA'). Quote 1 is on thesis p. 149 (PDF p. 34), §3.10.2 Disyllabic words, exactly: 'In disyllabic words, stress occurs on the first syllable irrespective of the internal structure of the constituent syllables.' Quote 2 is on thesis p. 169 (PDF p. 54), §3.13 summary items (b) and (d), exactly as reported; the only difference is a extracted text spacing artifact ('stress.In trisyllabic'). Surrounding sections read: §3.8 data (113-115) pp. 136-139 with wordlists (ˈba.ɽi 'home', ˈba.liʃ 'pillow', ˈhuk.na 'thin', ˈbai$.ɔn 'brinjal', u.ˈrus.xar 'prize',…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default primary stress on the initial syllable (left-headed syllabic trochees built left to right). Disyllables are always initially stressed whatever the weights (LL, LH, HL, HH). In trisyllables the initial (antepenult) is stressed unless it is light and the penult is heavy (closed syllable), in which case the penult takes primary stress (u.ˈrus.xar 'prize', pɔ.ˈrik.ka 'examination'); only closed syllables (VC, CVC, CVVC) count as heavy, diphthongs are monomoraic. The author summarises the parameters as trochee, left-to-right, head-left, 'partially quantity sensitive', with extrametricality (p. 147).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Two degrees of stress. A word-final heavy syllable after a primary foot forms its own foot with secondary stress: (ˈLL)(ˌH) e.g. (ˈɸɔ.ta)(ˌxal) 'dawn', and HHH gives (ˈHH)(ˌH) e.g. hɔ$.rɔk.kɔn 'reservation' (pp. 136-139, 143). Two successive heavy syllables never both carry stress (no clash).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is not contrastive (p. 146). Analysis restricted to monomorphemic di- and trisyllables because native words of 4-5 syllables are 'very rare' (p. 138-139). Author says SHB has no fixed rule like Hungarian/Polish but is not free either; possible positions limited (p. 169). A companion statement in Goswami 2021 (Acta Linguistica Asiatica 11(1): 109-110): 'The prominent stress pattern of SHB is disyllabic where the first syllable attracts stress, and SHB speakers prefer heavy syllables to be considered as stressed.' Note the separate tone literature (Gope & Mahanta 2014, 2016; Raychoudhury & Mahanta 2020; Raychoudhury 2023) treats Sylheti as a three-tone language and does not describe word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated content words (monomorphemic, non-compound), elicited from Sylheti speakers of North Tripura; impressionistic metrical analysis (tree/grid), no acoustic measurements of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Goswami's data are from "Sylheti speakers of North Tripura" (India), i.e. the Indian (Tripura/Barak Valley side) variety of Sylheti = sylh1242; she calls it "Sylheti Bangla (SHB)". The IIT Guwahati tone literature (Gope, Raychoudhury, Mahanta; Barak Valley and Bangladesh speakers) describes the same glottocode as a three-tone language and makes no word-stress claim; Raychoudhury 2023 explicitly leaves "rhythm and stress" for future study.

sources.note: Full metrical chapter (ch. 3, pp. 116-169): initial stress in all disyllables; trisyllables antepenult unless L-H-x, then penult; trochaic, left-to-right, partially quantity sensitive; secondary stress on a final heavy foot; stress not contrastive.
